Every year during the Thadingyut festival, you might see colorful lanterns and shimmering candles lighting up homes and streets. It is a joyful time, but there is also a beautiful story behind these lights. It is the story of how the Buddha showed his deep love and gratitude for his mother by sharing his most precious teachings with her.

Long ago, when the Buddha was still Prince Siddhartha, his mother, Queen Maya, passed away only seven days after he was born. She was reborn as a celestial being named Santussita in a heavenly realm. Even though they were separated for a long time, the Buddha never forgot her. Once he became enlightened, he looked for the best way to repay his mother for the gift of life.

During his seventh year as a teacher, the Buddha traveled to Tavatimsa Heaven. He sat under a great tree on a special throne made of emerald-colored stone. For three whole months during the rainy season, he preached the Abhidhamma, which is a very deep and detailed part of his teachings. He did this specifically to honor his mother and help her find peace.

Because the teaching lasted day and night for three months, the Buddha used his miraculous powers to create a Nimita Buddha:

- This was a perfect duplicate of himself that looked and spoke exactly like him.

- While the duplicate stayed in heaven to continue the sermon, the real Buddha would return to Earth each day to collect alms and eat.

- During these breaks, he taught a summary of the lessons to his chief disciple, Sariputta, so the wisdom could be shared with people on Earth too.

By the end of the three months, his mother had listened to the entire teaching and reached a high level of spiritual wisdom. Millions of other heavenly beings also found enlightenment. This was the greatest gift a child could ever give a parent because it helped her find lasting happiness.

If the Buddha, the greatest teacher in the world, took such care to honor his mother, we should try to follow his example. We can show gratitude to our parents by:

- Being kind.

- Listening to their advice.

- Helping them whenever they need us.

Being a respectful and loving child is the best way to bring light to your family, just like the glowing lanterns of Thadingyut.

The Full Moon Day of Thadingyut is a special time for many reasons. While you might know it as the Festival of Lights, it is also a very meaningful day for Buddhist monks called Pavarana Day. The word Pavarana comes from the Pali language and means "invitation" or "requesting advice." To understand why this day is so important, we have to look at how monks live during the rainy season.

Lesson
For three months, monks stay together in one monastery for their Rains Retreat. Living closely with others for a long time can sometimes lead to small misunderstandings or hidden frustrations. On Pavarana Day, before they travel to different places, the monks gather for a unique ceremony:

Lesson
- Instead of hiding their flaws, they bravely invite their fellow monks to speak up.

Lesson
- A monk might say: "If you have seen, heard, or suspected that I have done something wrong, please tell me out of kindness. I will admit my mistake and try to improve."

Lesson
The Buddha encouraged this tradition because he wanted his followers to live in harmony and unity. When people keep their worries or anger bottled up inside, it creates tension and distance between friends. By honestly admitting mistakes and listening to advice, everyone can clear their hearts of doubt. It takes great courage to admit when you are wrong, but it is the only way to become a better person. Having a friend who is willing to help you correct your mistakes is considered a great blessing.

This beautiful tradition eventually spread from the monasteries into the homes of everyday people. This is why we have the lovely custom of paying respect to our parents, grandparents, and teachers during Thadingyut.

1. When we bow to our elders, we ask for forgiveness for any unkind words or actions we may have used throughout the year.

2. When our elders forgive us with love, everyone feels a sense of peace and a fresh start.

You can practice the spirit of Pavarana in your own life too. Whether you are at school or playing with siblings, disagreements are bound to happen. If you realize you have made a mistake, have the courage to say, "I am sorry, I was wrong." If a friend comes to you to apologize, be kind enough to say, "I forgive you." Children who are honest about their mistakes and quick to forgive others will always find themselves surrounded by friends and living with a happy, peaceful heart.

Every year, after the beautiful Full Moon of Thadingyut, a wonderful tradition takes place across Myanmar. It is a time when people visit their parents, grandparents, teachers, and elderly neighbors to pay their respects. This special ceremony is a meaningful part of Myanmar culture that brings families and communities closer together.

This act of showing respect is called "Gadaw." When we Gadaw, we place our hands together and bow to show honor to those who are older and wiser. It is also a very important time to ask for forgiveness. If we were ever rude, disobedient, or made someone feel sad during the year, we apologize sincerely. This tradition is inspired by a monastic practice called "Pavarana," where monks invite each other to point out their mistakes so they can live in harmony. By following this example, we clear away any bad feelings and start fresh with love and kindness.

There are four main groups of people we should honor:

Lesson
1. Parents, who gave us life and took care of us.

2. Grandparents, who are the pillars of our families.

3. Teachers, who provide us with the knowledge and skills we need for the future.

Lesson
4. Elderly people living in our neighborhoods who have lived long, experienced lives.

When we visit these elders, it is polite to bring small offerings such as:

- Fruit and snacks

Lesson
- Clothing

- Fresh flowers

We should always present these gifts using both hands to show our deep respect. In return for this kindness, the elders give us their heartfelt blessings. They often wish for us to be healthy, happy, smart, and safe from danger. These words of wisdom and love are like a protective shield that stays with us as we grow.

Lesson
By practicing Gadaw, we develop two very special qualities: gratitude and humility.

- Gratitude means remembering the kindness others have shown us.

- Humility means being respectful and modest.

While Thadingyut is a famous time for these ceremonies, you can show respect every single day. You can do this by listening to your parents, helping your teachers, and being kind to the elderly people you meet. Being a respectful person is one of the best ways to lead a happy and successful life.
